questions.stem_md:
Your group's first `scripts/check.sh` ran the four checks on four lines and ended with `echo "Ready to tag"`. A teammate changes it:

```diff
diff --git a/scripts/check.sh b/scripts/check.sh
index 46245be..46862c3 100755
--- a/scripts/check.sh
+++ b/scripts/check.sh
@@ -1,6 +1,8 @@
 #!/usr/bin/env bash
+set -euo pipefail
+
 uv run ruff check .
 uv run ruff format --check .
 uv run mypy src tests
 uv run pytest -q
 echo "Ready to tag"
```

Two candidate commit messages:

- A: `Update check.sh`
- B: `Stop check.sh at the first failing check`
questions.explanation_md: The diff adds one line, so the question is what it changes in behaviour. Without `set -e` a script runs every line and exits with the last command's code. Run on a copy of the expense-tracker with a broken `largest_expense`, the old script printed `1 failed, 23 passed`, then `Ready to tag`, and exited 0; with the new line the same run stopped after pytest and exited 1. `-u` and `pipefail` change nothing in this script, which has no variables and no pipelines. Message B tells a future reader the behaviour that changed; A only names the file. The test is session 8's habit: see it fail first.
questions.source_ref: midterm sample Q8 (compare shape); partial rubric 'Check yourself'; S10 slide 16; run on a copy of expense-tracker v0.4 (pipes-bash-fix/runs/compare-U8.diff, nosete-test.out, sete-test.out)

parts.prompt_md: What does this change do? Say what the script did before when a check failed, and what it does now.
parts.model_answer_md: Before, every line ran and the script exited with the `echo`'s code, so a failed check still printed Ready to tag and exited 0. Now the first failing check stops the script with a non-zero exit, and Ready to tag appears only when all four pass.
rubric: Before: every line ran and the exit code was the `echo`'s, so a failed check still ended in 0 and Ready to tag
After: stops at the first non-zero exit and exits non-zero; Ready to tag only when all four checks pass
parts.weak_answers_md: "It makes the script safer" or "it adds error handling" names no mechanism. Many answers describe only the new behaviour and miss what was wrong before: the old script ended with `echo`, so its exit code was 0 whatever ruff, mypy or pytest said. Saying the old script "stopped at the error anyway" is the misconception the change fixes.

parts.prompt_md: Which message is better for someone reading the history six months later, and why?
parts.model_answer_md: B. It says what behaviour changed, so a reader knows why the commit exists without opening the diff. A only names the file, which the diff already shows.
rubric: Chooses B
Reason: B states the behaviour that changed; A says nothing the list of changed files does not already say
parts.weak_answers_md: "B is longer" or "B is more detailed" gives no reason; length is beside the point. The mark is for saying what B tells a future reader that A does not: what the script now does differently. Choosing A because "the diff explains it" forgets that `git log --oneline` shows only the messages.

parts.prompt_md: Describe in words one check you would run to show the change works.
parts.model_answer_md: Make one check fail on purpose, say an unused import, run the script and confirm it stops there with no Ready to tag and a non-zero `echo $?`. Then undo it and confirm the clean run still ends with Ready to tag and 0.
rubric: Breaks a check on purpose and expects the script to stop with a non-zero exit code (no Ready to tag)
Also confirms the clean case still passes with exit 0
parts.weak_answers_md: "Run it and see if it passes" proves nothing: the old script also passed on clean code. The test that shows the change is the failing case, as in session 8's red step: make it fail first, then check the exit code as well as the screen. Testing only the failing case and never the clean one gets half.

questions.stem_md:
Your group's first `scripts/check.sh`:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
uv run ruff check .
uv run ruff format --check .
uv run mypy src tests
uv run pytest -q
echo "Ready to tag"
```

After a teammate changes `largest_expense`, you run it (trimmed):

```console
$ ./scripts/check.sh
All checks passed!
7 files already formatted
Success: no issues found in 6 source files
....................F...                                                 [100%]
...
FAILED tests/test_report.py::test_largest_expense_tie_goes_to_the_first - Ass...
1 failed, 23 passed in 0.05s
Ready to tag
$ echo $?
0
```

Why does the script exit 0 although a test failed?
questions.explanation_md: A script without `set -e` runs every line, like commands joined by `;`, and exits with the code of the last command that ran. Here pytest exited 1 (checked by running `uv run pytest -q` on its own), then `echo "Ready to tag"` ran and exited 0, so the script exited 0 and printed a message that is false. Anything that trusts the exit code sees green. Session 5: "A program that prints an error and exits 0 is a program that lies." With `set -euo pipefail` on line 2, the same run stopped after pytest, printed no `Ready to tag` and exited 1 (run).
questions.source_ref: S5 slide 9; partial rubric 'Check yourself'; S10 slide 16; run on a copy of expense-tracker v0.4 with a broken largest_expense (pipes-bash-fix/runs/nosete-test.out, sete-test.out, lint.out)

options.text_md: pytest exits 0 when most tests pass; only a run where every test fails counts as a failure
options.why_md: Run on its own here, `uv run pytest -q` exits 1: one failing test is enough. The 1 was there; the script threw it away.

options.text_md: Without `set -e` every line runs, and the script exits with its last command's code: the `echo`
options.why_md: Right: the lines behave like commands joined by `;`. pytest exited 1, then `echo` ran and exited 0, and that is what the script reports.

options.text_md: `uv run` hides the exit code of the tool it starts and always hands 0 back to the script
options.why_md: `uv run` passes the tool's exit code on: `uv run ruff check .` exits 1 when ruff finds a problem, which is what CI's Lint step relies on.

options.text_md: A script's exit code comes from its first command, and ruff reported that all checks passed
options.why_md: It is the last command that counts. Had ruff failed instead, this script would still have exited 0, because `echo` ran last.

You meant to count the dining lines but pressed Enter too early. The prompt does not come back, so you type the file name as well:

```console
$ grep dining
expenses.csv
```

Still nothing happens. What is going on?
questions.explanation_md: Programs that read text take it from a file name or, when given none, from stdin. Nothing was piped or redirected, so stdin is the keyboard: grep waits for lines and prints back any that contain `dining`. Typing `expenses.csv` gave it one line of text with no `dining` in it, so it printed nothing. Run for real in an interactive bash: typing `2025-07-10,Federal Cafe,dining,53.82` made grep print that line back, and Ctrl-C stopped it (`echo $?` then showed 130). options.text_md: grep is searching every file on the disk for `dining`, which takes a while; wait for it
options.why_md: grep never goes looking for files on its own. With no file name it reads stdin, so waiting changes nothing.

options.text_md: grep is reading stdin, the keyboard, and searching what you type; Ctrl-C stops it
options.why_md: Right: `expenses.csv` was read as a line of text to search, and it contains no `dining`. Ctrl-C (session 9) stops the program.

options.text_md: grep crashed because the file name was missing, and the terminal froze; open a new window
options.why_md: Nothing crashed: grep is running and waiting for input. Ctrl-C stops it without losing the terminal.

options.text_md: grep is waiting for its file name and will open `expenses.csv` once you press Enter again

On the sample file (5 dining, 3 transport and 2 home expenses; one dining merchant is called `Sushi at home`):

```console
$ grep -c dining expenses.csv > counts.txt
$ grep -c transport expenses.csv >> counts.txt
$ grep -c home expenses.csv > counts.txt
$ cat counts.txt
```

What does the last command print?
questions.explanation_md: `>` empties the file before the command runs; `>>` adds to the end. After the second command `counts.txt` held `5` and `3` (checked with `cat`). The third command uses `>` again, so the shell empties the file and grep writes a single number. That number is 3: grep counts lines that contain `home` anywhere, and `2025-07-06,Sushi at home,dining,24.90` is one of them. Run for real, `cat counts.txt` printed `3`. To collect several counts in one file, every command after the first needs `>>`.

options.why_md: Right: the third `>` emptied the file and grep wrote one number: the 3 lines that contain `home`, Sushi at home included.

options.text_md: `5`, `3` and `3`, one per line
options.why_md: That needs `>>` on the third line too. `>` replaces the file every time, whatever wrote to it before.
The file was replaced, but `grep -c home` counts lines that contain `home` anywhere: 3 lines for 2 home expenses.

options.text_md: `5`, `3` and `2`, one per line
options.why_md: Two slips at once: the third `>` replaces the file instead of adding to it, and grep counts 3 lines for the 2 home expenses.

questions.stem_md:
You add two expenses, one with a comma in the merchant name, and look at the categories with a pipeline:

```console
$ uv run expenses add "Bar Ramon" dining 9.80 --date 2025-12-30
added Bar Ramon (dining) 9.80 to data/expenses.csv
$ uv run expenses add "Can Recasens, Gracia" dining 33.02 --date 2025-12-31
added Can Recasens, Gracia (dining) 33.02 to data/expenses.csv
$ cat data/expenses.csv
date,merchant,category,amount
2025-12-30,Bar Ramon,dining,9.80
2025-12-31,"Can Recasens, Gracia",dining,33.02
$ tail -n +2 data/expenses.csv | cut -d, -f3
dining
 Gracia"
```

`uv run expenses report data/expenses.csv` shows both under dining, 42.82 in total. What explains the second line of cut's output?
questions.explanation_md: `cut -d, -f3` knows nothing about CSV: it splits each line at every comma. `add` writes with Python's `csv` module, which puts quotes around a merchant name that contains a comma, so that row has one comma more than the others and its third field is ` Gracia"`. The program reads the file with `csv.reader`, which respects the quotes, so the report shows dining 42.82 for both (run). Text tools give quick answers on simple files like the course's `expenses.csv`; when a field can contain the separator, trust the tested code. Same habit as the merchant trap: check a pipeline's answer against something you know.
questions.source_ref: expense-tracker v0.4 cli.py (add uses csv.writer); S10 slides 6–8; run on a fresh clone of expense-tracker v0.4 (pipes-bash-fix/runs/comma.out)

options.text_md: `add` saved the row wrongly: the quotes are a bug, and the report total is wrong too
options.why_md: The quotes are how CSV keeps a comma inside one field; Python's `csv` writer added them on purpose, and the report reads them back correctly.

options.text_md: `tail -n +2` broke the long line in two, and cut printed the end of the second half
options.why_md: tail works on whole lines; it never splits one. The line reached cut intact, with one comma more than the others.

options.text_md: The quotes shift every row by one field, so the category is now field 4 in all rows
options.why_md: Only the row with the comma has an extra field. Bar Ramon's row still gave `dining` from field 3.

options.text_md: cut splits at every comma, even inside quotes; the program's CSV reader does not
options.why_md: Right: for cut the quoted name is two fields, so field 3 is ` Gracia"`. `csv.reader` understands the quotes.

questions.stem_md:
In an empty folder:

```console
$ echo start > log.txt
$ echo checks passed >> log.txt
$ echo checks passed >> log.txt
$ cat log.txt
```

What does the last command print?
questions.explanation_md: `>` replaces the content of a file, `>>` appends to it. The first line creates `log.txt` holding `start`. The next two each add `checks passed` at the end, so the file has three lines and `cat` prints them in that order. Had the second line used `>`, the file would have held only `checks passed` once, because `>` empties the file before the command runs. Run for real, `cat log.txt` printed the three lines.
questions.source_ref: S10 slides 5, 9; run on the sample file (calibration-fix/pb)

options.text_md: `checks passed`, once, because the second `>>` replaces the first line
options.why_md: `>>` never replaces anything. It adds the output to the end of the file, whatever is already there.

options.text_md: `start`, `checks passed` and `checks passed`, one per line
options.why_md: Right: the first command creates the file with `start`, and each `>>` adds one line at the end. Three lines in all.

options.text_md: `start` and `checks passed`, because the same line is not written twice
options.why_md: Nothing removes duplicates here. Dropping repeated lines is the job of `sort | uniq`, not of a redirection.

options.text_md: `checks passed` twice, because the first `>>` replaced `start`
options.why_md: Replacing is what a single `>` does. `>>` keeps what is already in the file and appends.

questions.stem_md:
On the sample file:

```console
$ head -3 expenses.csv > small.csv
$ sort < small.csv > sorted.csv
$ cat sorted.csv
```

What does `cat sorted.csv` print?
questions.explanation_md: `sort < small.csv` hands the file to `sort` on its standard input, so it behaves like `sort small.csv`, and `> sorted.csv` sends the result to a file instead of the screen: the command prints nothing. `sort` orders every line, and the header is just a line. Digits come before letters, so the two rows starting with `2025-` go first and `date,merchant,category,amount` goes last. That is why a pipeline that sorts a CSV usually drops the header first with `tail -n +2`. Run for real, the file held the two rows and then the header.

options.text_md: The header, then the two expense rows, in date order
options.why_md: `sort` knows nothing about headers. It orders all three lines as plain text, header included.

options.text_md: The three lines of `small.csv` unchanged, because `sort` only works on a file name
options.why_md: `<` feeds the file to `sort` on stdin, and `sort` reads stdin when it has no file name. It sorts exactly as before.

options.text_md: Nothing: the `>` empties `small.csv` before `sort` can read it
options.why_md: The output goes to a different file, `sorted.csv`. Reading and writing the same file in one command is the trap, not this one.

options.text_md: The two expense rows, then the header line, because lines starting with a digit sort first
options.why_md: Right: `sort` compares whole lines, and a line starting with `2` comes before one starting with `d`. The header ends up last.

questions.stem_md:
On the sample file, `small.csv` holds the header and the first two expenses, and `nosuch.csv` does not exist. The shell applies redirections from left to right: each one points a stream at wherever its target points at that moment. So in `> all.txt 2>&1`, stdout goes to the file first, and `2>&1` then sends stderr to wherever stdout now goes.

```console
$ cat small.csv nosuch.csv > all.txt 2>&1
$ cat all.txt
```

What appears on the screen when the first command runs, and what does `all.txt` hold?
questions.explanation_md: `cat` writes the three lines of `small.csv` (the header and two expenses) to stdout, and its complaint about the missing file to stderr. `> all.txt` points stdout at the file. `2>&1` then points stderr at wherever stdout points, which is now the file, so the screen stays empty and `all.txt` gets both. The exit code is still 1, because the second file failed. Run for real, `cat all.txt` showed the three CSV lines and then the `cat:` error. This is the usual way to keep a whole log of a command in one file.
questions.source_ref: extension of S10 slide 5 (2>&1 is not on the slides); run on the sample file (calibration-fix/pb)

options.text_md: Nothing on the screen; `all.txt` holds the three CSV lines, then `cat: nosuch.csv: No such file or directory`
options.why_md: Right: both streams go to the file, in the order `cat` produced them. The error comes last because the second file is read last.

options.text_md: The error on the screen; `all.txt` holds the three CSV lines
options.why_md: That is what `> all.txt` alone does, because only stdout is redirected. With `2>&1` after it, stderr follows stdout into the file.

options.text_md: The three CSV lines on the screen; `all.txt` holds the error message only
options.why_md: It reverses the streams: the CSV lines are stdout and go to the file, and the error is stderr.

options.text_md: Nothing on the screen; `all.txt` holds only the CSV lines, because `2>&1` sends the error back to the screen
options.why_md: `&1` means 'where stdout points now', and stdout already points at `all.txt`. It does not mean the screen.

questions.stem_md:
The first lines of the group's `scripts/check.sh`:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
uv run ruff check .
```

A teammate runs `./scripts/check.sh`. What is the job of the first line?
questions.explanation_md: A bash script starts with `#!/usr/bin/env bash`, the shebang. When you run `./scripts/check.sh`, the system reads that first line and starts `bash` with the file as its input, so the script runs the same from a zsh terminal, from CI or from another script. It does not grant the right to run the file: that is the `x` permission, which `chmod +x` adds and git records. It also does not stop the script on errors; that needs `set -e`.
questions.source_ref: S10 slides 12, 14; S9 permissions

options.text_md: It makes the file executable, so nobody needs to run `chmod +x`
options.why_md: Permission is a property of the file, set with `chmod`. The first line is only text inside the file.

options.text_md: It makes the script stop at the first command that fails
options.why_md: That is `set -e`, a line of its own. The first line says which program runs the file.

options.text_md: It loads the tools the script uses, so that `uv` and `ruff` are found
options.why_md: Nothing is loaded. Commands are found through the `PATH`, as they are in any shell.

options.text_md: It tells the system to run the file with bash, whatever shell the caller is using
options.why_md: Right: the two characters `#!` followed by a program name say 'start this program and give it the file'.

questions.stem_md:
`count.sh` counts the rows of the file you give it:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
FILE=$1
echo "Rows in $FILE: $(wc -l < "$FILE")"
```

Run with a file name it prints `Rows in expenses.csv: 19`. Run with no argument:

```console
$ ./count.sh
./count.sh: line 3: $1: unbound variable
$ echo $?
1
```

Why did it stop there?
questions.explanation_md: `set -u` makes bash treat reading an unset variable as an error. With no argument, line 3 reads `$1`, which was never set, so the script stops with `unbound variable` and exit code 1, before `wc` is started. Without `set -u`, `FILE` would be empty, `wc` would be given nothing to read and the script would carry on: it printed `No such file or directory` and then a line saying `Rows in :` with no number. A script that fails at the first missing input is easier to trust than one that goes on with empty values. Run for real, both versions behaved as shown.
questions.source_ref: S10 slide 16; run in calibration-fix/pb

options.text_md: `set -u` stops bash when a script reads a variable that was never set, here `$1`; without it the script would go on with an empty `FILE`
options.why_md: Right: no argument means `$1` was never set. Without `set -u` the script would run on and fail later, or print a wrong line.

options.text_md: `$1` cannot be used in a script that has `set -u`, so every script with it must avoid arguments
options.why_md: `$1` works fine when an argument is given, as the first run shows. The error is about an unset value.

options.text_md: `set -u` checks that the file exists before the script runs, and `expenses.csv` was missing
options.why_md: No file name was given at all, and `set -u` checks variables, not files.

options.text_md: `wc -l` failed on the missing file, and `set -u` turned its error into an unbound variable message
options.why_md: `wc` never ran. The message names `$1` and line 3, the line before `wc`.

Slide 19 shows one trap of `set -e`. This script exits at the `((counter++))` line, silently, and never prints `reached`:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e
counter=0
((counter++))
echo "reached"
```

Why?
questions.explanation_md: `((expression))` is a command whose exit status is 0 when the expression is non-zero and 1 when it is zero. `counter++` evaluates to the old value, so with `counter=0` the status is 1 (run: `status=1 counter=1`: the counter did increase). `set -e` treats the 1 as a failing command and stops the script. Use `counter=$((counter + 1))`, which is an expansion, not a command, and is safe (run: `status=0`). The stop itself is what slide 19 and lab 10b exercise 4 describe on Ubuntu's bash; macOS's old bash 3.2 does not stop there.
questions.source_ref: S10 slide 19; labs/10-bash.md exercise 4; exit statuses run in bash (runs/sample_extra.out)

options.text_md: `counter` was never declared, and `set -e` stops a script that uses an undeclared variable
options.why_md: `counter=0` sets it. Variables need no declaration, and catching unset variables is the job of `set -u`.

options.text_md: `++` is not valid in bash, so the shell reports a syntax error and leaves
options.why_md: `((counter++))` is valid and it does add one to `counter`. The problem is its exit status, not its syntax.

options.text_md: `((counter++))` evaluates to the old value, `0`, which counts as false; `set -e` reads that as a failing command and stops
options.why_md: Right: slide 19. `0` inside `(( ))` is false, so the command exits non-zero, even though `counter` did become 1.

options.text_md: `counter=0` already failed, because an assignment exits 1 when it stores a zero
options.why_md: An assignment exits 0. The failing line is the arithmetic command that follows it.

items.why_md: That is the default. `-o pipefail` changes it: the pipeline fails if any stage fails.

questions.stem_md:
A teammate saves a pipeline as `top.sh`:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
if [ "$#" -lt 1 ]; then
  echo "usage: $0 FILE" >&2
  exit 2
fi
if [ ! -f "$1" ]; then
  echo "error: $1 is not a file" >&2
  exit 1
fi
tail -n +2 "$1" | cut -d, -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3
```

Three runs, in the folder with the course's `expenses.csv`:

```console
$ ./top.sh expenses.csv
    119 groceries
     86 dining
     76 transport
$ ./top.sh; echo $?
usage: ./top.sh FILE
2
$ ./top.sh nofile; echo $?
error: nofile is not a file
1
```
questions.explanation_md: This is slides 12, 14 and 15 in one script. A strong answer reads the pipeline stage by stage (the same skill as sample question 6), separates the two kinds of error by the problem they catch, and knows that the exit code is what the caller reads. Run for real: `./top.sh nofile > out.txt` printed the error on the screen and `out.txt` had 0 lines, and `./top.sh "Moodle Files/expenses.csv"` worked because the argument is quoted.
questions.source_ref: S10 slides 12, 14–15; run (runs/s10_top.out)

parts.prompt_md: Say in words what the last line of the script does, stage by stage, and what the three lines of output tell you.
parts.model_answer_md: `tail -n +2` drops the header, `cut -d, -f3` keeps the category, `sort` puts equal names together, `uniq -c` counts each group, `sort -rn` puts the biggest count first and `head -n 3` keeps three. The output: groceries has the most expenses (119), then dining (86) and transport (76).
rubric: The stages in order: drop the header, keep the category column, sort, count each group, rank by count, keep the top three
Reads the output: the three categories with the most expenses, and how many each has
parts.weak_answers_md: "It finds the top three" says what it is for and skips the stages. Many answers forget that the header is removed first, or say `uniq -c` counts all the duplicates without noting that `sort` must come before it. The output lines are counts of expenses, not euros.

parts.prompt_md: The two error calls print different messages and different exit codes. What does each test catch, and why does the script use 2 and 1?
parts.model_answer_md: The first test catches a call with no argument: the script was used wrongly, so it prints a usage line and exits 2. The second catches an argument that is not a file: the job cannot be done, so it prints an error and exits 1. Both are failures to `&&`, `set -e` and CI, which read the number.
rubric: Two different problems: no argument (usage) and an argument that is not a file
Any non-zero code is a failure that the next command or CI reads; the number says which kind (2 wrong call, 1 failed job)
parts.weak_answers_md: Answers that say 2 means "worse" than 1, or that only 1 is a failure, miss the point: every non-zero number is a failure and the choice is a convention. "So the user can read it" ignores that the reader is the next program, not a person.

parts.prompt_md: Why are both messages written with `>&2`, and what are the quotes in `"$1"` for?
parts.model_answer_md: `>&2` sends the message to stderr, so `./top.sh nofile > out.txt` leaves `out.txt` empty and the message still reaches the person. The quotes keep a path with a space, such as `Moodle Files/expenses.csv`, as one argument.
rubric: stderr keeps the message out of redirected output or a pipe, while the person still sees it
Quotes keep a value that contains spaces as a single word
parts.weak_answers_md: "To show errors in red" is wrong: stderr has no colour. "To print it faster" is not a reason either. Answers about quotes that say they "make it a string" miss the spaces: without quotes the shell splits the path into two words.
